title: The Sword and the Plowshare
subtitle: The long argument the church has had with itself about the sword, and the two great faithful traditions that argument produced.
question: When the world burns, may the people of the crucified God pick up the sword, and if they may, what has the cross already cost them before they do?
whyItMatters: The church has never settled this. For two thousand years the body of Christ has carried within it two answers to the sword, and both have produced saints, and both have produced martyrs, and both can read the same Gospel and arrive at opposite ends of the rifle. This is not a fringe dispute. It is the question of whether the kingdom that comes by a man dying rather than killing can be defended by killing, and the church has answered yes and no in the same century, sometimes in the same pew.
biblicalFoundation: Begin where Jesus begins. On the mountain he blesses the peacemakers and calls them sons of God, and a few breaths later he tells the crowd to love their enemies and to turn the other cheek and to pray for the ones who persecute them. He does not soften it. He does not add an asterisk for national emergencies. The Sermon on the Mount is the most quoted and least obeyed text in the church's possession, and the reason is simple. It costs everything to take it at its word, and it costs the conscience something to explain it away.

But the same scriptures that bless the peacemaker also describe a God who goes to war. The prophets Isaiah and Micah see a day when the nations beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks and study war no more, and that vision is given as a promise, not a present command. The wars of the Old Testament are real and bloody and commanded, and the church has never been able to pretend they are not there. Christians have read those wars in the light of Christ, as belonging to a particular people at a particular hour in the long story that finds its end in him, and the honest reader admits that this reading carries weight and also carries unfinished business.

Then there is Romans 13, where Paul says the governing authority bears the sword for a reason and does not bear it in vain, that the magistrate is God's servant to execute wrath on the wrongdoer. The just-war tradition has stood on this verse for sixteen centuries. The peace tradition answers that the same Paul, two sentences earlier, forbids the Christian to take revenge and commands him to leave wrath to God and to overcome evil with good. Both are reading Paul. Both are reading him carefully. The text holds the tension and refuses to release it.

And at the center stands the Prince of Peace, who could have called down legions of angels and did not, who told Peter to put up his sword in the garden because those who live by it die by it, who conquered not by killing his enemies but by dying for them. The cross is the place where the power of the sword is both judged and absorbed. Whatever a Christian finally concludes about war, he concludes it standing in front of a man who refused to save himself by force. That refusal is not a footnote to the Gospel. It is the Gospel.
keyTexts: Matthew 5:9, 38 to 44 (blessed are the peacemakers, turn the other cheek, love your enemies)
Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 (they shall beat their swords into plowshares)
Romans 12:17 to 21 and 13:1 to 4 (overcome evil with good, the magistrate bears the sword)
Matthew 26:52 (those who take the sword will perish by the sword)
Luke 22:36 to 38 (let the one who has no sword buy one) read against John 18:36 (my kingdom is not of this world)
Revelation 19:11 to 15 (the rider whose only weapon is the sword of his mouth)

churchRecord.led: For the first three centuries the church was reluctant to take up arms at all, and many of its teachers told baptized men that the trade of killing did not belong to followers of the Lamb. When that reluctance gave way, the better minds of the church built a fence around the violence rather than blessing it freely. Augustine and later Aquinas worked out a tradition that asked hard questions before a sword could be drawn at all, just cause, right authority, right intention, last resort, and proportion, and that tradition has restrained as much blood as it has permitted. Alongside it the peace churches kept the other half of the witness alive. The Anabaptists died rather than carry weapons, the Quakers refused the oath and the musket and built whole colonies on the refusal, and in the wars that followed there were chaplains who carried no rifle into the trenches and protesters who carried no rifle into the streets, and both believed they were obeying the same Lord.
churchRecord.failed: And the church has also blessed what it should have buried. It preached the Crusades and called the slaughter holy and promised heaven for the killing. It has sanctified nearly every national war its members happened to be fighting, blessing the guns on both sides of the same front while each side sang to the same God. It has too often reduced the office of chaplain from a ministry of mercy to a chaplaincy of militarism, a priesthood that consecrates the state's violence and asks no questions. When the flag and the cross hang at the same height in the sanctuary, the church has usually surrendered something it will not get back by apologizing later.

whereWeAgree: Every faithful tradition in this argument longs for peace and confesses that Christ is the Prince of Peace. No Christian who has read the Sermon on the Mount can pretend that war is good, or that the peace of the kingdom comes through the barrel of a gun. We agree that the final word belongs to the one who beats swords into plowshares, and that any sword a Christian ever lifts is lifted under judgment and never under celebration.
captureLeft: The left capture is a pacifism that has lost its nerve to be honest. It condemns its own nation's wars with prophetic fury and goes silent before the wars and atrocities of regimes it finds ideologically convenient, which is not pacifism but partisanship wearing the clothes of the Lamb. It can be naive about real evil, treating tyranny and genocide as misunderstandings to be talked down rather than horrors that have crushed millions of actual bodies. It can collapse into a reflexive posture in which the soldier is suspect, the West is always the aggressor, and the only sin worth naming is the one committed by people who look like us.
captureRight: The right capture is the baptizing of the sword. It drapes the sanctuary in the flag and treats the armed forces as a branch of the faith, fusing God and country until no one can tell where worship ends and patriotism begins. It treats peacemaking as weakness and the Sermon on the Mount as private sentiment that has no business near foreign policy. It has never met a national war it would not bless, and it mistakes the willingness to kill for the measure of conviction, forgetting that the Lord it claims conquered by being killed.
whereWeDiffer: Here is what an honest church admits. The just-war tradition and the pacifist tradition are both ancient, both faithful, both born from the scriptures and tested by the blood of saints, and neither one is the obvious cowardice or the obvious compromise the other side accuses it of being. Christians who fear God and love the cross land in both. And the justice of any specific war is genuinely contested, not because Christians are evasive but because the questions the tradition asks, just cause and last resort and proportion, are brutally hard to answer in real time with real lives in the balance. The person who finds these questions easy has not understood them.
theCost: The cost of taking this seriously is that you lose the comfort of belonging cleanly to a side. The Christian who holds to just war must live with the knowledge that he has blessed killing and may have blessed it wrongly. The Christian who holds to nonviolence must live with the knowledge that his refusal may leave the weak undefended and the tyrant unopposed. There is no posture here that keeps your hands clean and your conscience quiet. I have wanted one. I have wanted a position that let me feel righteous about other people's wars without the weight of my own complicity, and that position does not exist. We are all standing in front of the cross with blood somewhere on us, and the only question is whether we will be honest about it.
charge: Refuse the easy capture, whichever one tempts you. If your politics already told you what God thinks about every war before you opened the scriptures, your politics is your god. Sit in the tension the church has carried for two thousand years. Honor the just-war Christian and the peace-church Christian as your brother and not your enemy, and reserve your hardest words for the moment when you catch your own tribe baptizing its sword. Then go and be a peacemaker, which Jesus said was a hard and blessed thing, and which has never once meant doing nothing.

right.label: The Baptized Sword
right.whatItLooksLike: Faith and the armed forces fused until the gun is holy and the dissenter is a traitor. The sanctuary becomes an extension of the state, the Sermon on the Mount becomes private feeling, and the willingness to kill becomes the proof of conviction.
right.inThePast: The church preached the Crusades and promised heaven for the slaughter. It blessed the guns of empire and called colonial conquest mission. In nearly every modern war the churches on both sides consecrated their own nation's cause and sang to the same God across the same trenches.
right.now: A civil religion that hangs the flag higher than the cross, that reads American power as divine mandate, that treats any restraint on the military as a betrayal of faith, and that cannot imagine a Christian who questions a war.
named: civil-religion militarism that fuses God and country in the sanctuary
the historic blessing of national wars on every side at once
the consecration of the Crusades and colonial conquest as holy
the flag-draped sanctuary where patriotism replaces worship
the treatment of peacemaking and conscientious objection as weakness or betrayal
the chaplaincy reduced to a priesthood that consecrates the state's violence
the fusion of evangelical identity with reflexive support for the armed forces

left.label: The Selective Peace
left.whatItLooksLike: A pacifism that is really a partisanship, loud against its own nation's wars and silent before the atrocities of regimes it finds congenial. It is naive about tyranny, suspicious of the soldier, and certain the West is always the aggressor.
left.inThePast: Movements that excused or minimized the violence of communist regimes while condemning only Western force, treating genocide abroad as Western propaganda and the only real sin as the one committed at home.
left.now: A reflexive anti-military and anti-Western posture that mistakes contempt for one's own country for the peace of Christ, that cannot name evil when an inconvenient party commits it, and that treats the soldier as the problem and the tyrant as a grievance to be understood.
named: a selective and one-sided pacifism that condemns only its own nation's wars
a reflexive anti-military posture that treats the soldier as suspect
a reflexive anti-Western framing in which the West is always the aggressor
a naivety about real evil, tyranny, and genocide as horrors to be explained away
the historic excusing or minimizing of atrocities by ideologically convenient regimes
the collapse of nonviolence into partisanship wearing the clothes of the Lamb
the reduction of peacemaking to doing nothing while the weak are crushed
